1331.title: Panja Sahib
1331.hook: the gurdwara of the handprint at Hasan Abdal
1331.howItsDone: Pilgrims who visit Gurdwara Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal place their hands in the handprint on the rock and take water from the spring that flows beneath it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kartarpur Sahib, where Guru Nanak farmed, and his hymn of the mind as farmer and the body as field. Your line was where he farmed.

Clear water slides out from under a rock, into a stone channel, and on into a wide tank where fish turn lazily in the light. One by one, pilgrims kneel, reach out, and fit a hand into a shape pressed into the rock above the water. Some hold it there a long moment. Some laugh because their hand is smaller. Some close their eyes. This is Hasan Abdal, in the hills of northern Pakistan, and the gurdwara is Panja Sahib. Year one told the story of the rock. Today, the water.
screen: `WATER FROM UNDER A ROCK.` → `A HAND FITTED INTO STONE.` → `TODAY, THE WATER.`

segments.voice: First, the story in one breath. Tradition says Guru Nanak and Mardana came to the hill thirsty. Mardana climbed three times to ask for water from the spring of a holy man at the top, Wali Qandhari, and three times came down with nothing. Nanak had him lift a stone at the foot of the hill, and water came up. A boulder came rolling down. Nanak stopped it with his open palm, and his hand, the story says, stayed in the stone. Panja means the palm of the hand. Second, where the water went. Refused at the top, it came up at the bottom, where the thirsty men sat, and it still flows there today, under the handprint and past the pilgrims. Third, why water matters so much here. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that the Guru has given him one understanding: there is one giver for every living being, and may he never forget that one. Water is about as plain a gift as there is, and in the story nobody owns the giver. Fourth, how to hold the hilltop. Sikhs read this story in more than one way, some as a miracle, some as a picture. People remember Wali Qandhari differently from the story, and a shrine to him still stands on the hill above, where visitors climb too. So the place keeps both: a shrine on the hill, a gurdwara at its foot, and water running between. What a pilgrim takes away is the shape of the hand: open, steady, where the thirsty were given a drink.
screen: `THREE CLIMBS, AND NOTHING.` · `REFUSED ABOVE, RISING BELOW.` · `ONE GIVER FOR EVERY LIVING BEING.` · `A SHRINE ABOVE, A GURDWARA BELOW.` · then, large: `THE HANDPRINT.`

segments.voice: Lay one hand flat on a table, your knee, or the floor, fingers spread, nothing gripped. Breathe in and notice it's steady; breathe out and notice it's open. Keep the palm open while you think of someone thirsty for something you could give: time, a call, a glass of water, a kind word.
Panja Sahib. The gurdwara at Hasan Abdal where pilgrims fit their hands into the print of Guru Nanak's palm, with water flowing beneath it. Today's word.
Your line: the handprint. An open hand, low enough to reach the thirsty. One more day on the hill.

1332.title: Anandpur Sahib
1332.hook: the city of bliss, the Khalsa's birthplace
1332.howItsDone: Sikhs visit Anandpur Sahib all year, especially Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, and gather there in large numbers for Hola Mohalla, with kirtan, langar and displays of martial skill.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal, the handprint in the rock and the water beneath it. Your line was the handprint.

A town's name can be a promise. This one is Anandpur, the city of bliss, tucked against low green hills in Punjab. At Hola Mohalla it fills up: drums, horses kicking up dust, blue and saffron banners, riders showing off old skills in an open field, and kitchens feeding everyone who comes. Sikhs remember it as the place where the Khalsa was born. And in Sikh memory it also knew sieges and hunger. A city of bliss, and a city of hard days. How can both be true of one place?
screen: `ANANDPUR: THE CITY OF BLISS.` → `DRUMS, HORSES, BANNERS.` → `BLISS, AND HARD DAYS.`

segments.voice: Start with how it began. Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, founded the town in the hills, and it became the home of his son, Guru Gobind Singh. Then its great day. Sikhs remember that here, at a Vaisakhi gathering, Guru Gobind Singh asked who would give their head, and from those who stood up he formed the Khalsa, the Guru's own. Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib stands where tradition places that day, one of the Takhts, the seats of Sikh authority. Then the hard part. Anandpur didn't stay peaceful. Tradition remembers armies around the town, hunger inside it, and the night the Guru's household left and was scattered on the road. Tomorrow's place belongs to that road. So why call it bliss? The Anand Sahib is a hymn of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, and Sikhs sing it at weddings and other gatherings. It opens, in paraphrase, with a voice telling its mother: I am in bliss, because I have found the True Guru. The bliss in the hymn isn't a calm afternoon or a good harvest. It comes from meeting the Guru. Anand is not the absence of trouble; it is the Guru's presence. That's how a town that knew sieges can carry the name city of bliss without any irony. Today Anandpur Sahib is a town of gurdwaras, quiet most days and packed at Hola Mohalla. The hills behind it are the same hills.
screen: `FOUNDED IN THE HILLS.` · `WHERE THE KHALSA WAS BORN.` · `SIEGE, HUNGER, LEAVING.` · `ANAND: THE GURU'S PRESENCE.` · then, large: `CITY OF BLISS.`

segments.voice: See a ring of low green hills, a river below, a town at their feet. Let the town get loud, drums, horses, kitchens smoking, and then let it go quiet, one lamp in a window, while the hills stay steady behind it all. If you pray, rest with the opening of the Anand Sahib; if not, just rest with the hills.
Anandpur Sahib. The city of bliss in the hills of Punjab, where Sikhs remember the Khalsa was born, and where Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib stands. Today's word.
Your line: city of bliss. Joy can live in a place that has known hard days. I'll be here tomorrow.

1333.title: Fatehgarh Sahib
1333.hook: where the younger Sahibzade were killed
1333.howItsDone: Sikhs visit Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib and the Thanda Burj to remember the younger Sahibzade and Mata Gujri, and gather there each winter for the Shaheedi Jor Mel, with kirtan, Ardas and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anandpur Sahib, the city of bliss in the hills, where Sikhs remember the Khalsa was born. Your line was city of bliss.

A small brick tower, open to the wind. Sikhs call it the Thanda Burj, the cold tower. Tradition says that after the Guru's household scattered on the road from Anandpur, Mata Gujri, the Tenth Guru's mother, was held here through winter nights with her two youngest grandsons. Today a gurdwara stands at that spot, and close by stands another, larger one: Fatehgarh Sahib. Sikhs visit this place quietly. So today goes slowly, and gently.
screen: `THE COLD TOWER.` → `A GRANDMOTHER AND TWO BOYS.` → `GO SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: First, who they were. The two younger sons of Guru Gobind Singh, Baba Zorawar Singh and Baba Fateh Singh, are called the younger Sahibzade, the sons of the master. Sikh memory says they were brought before the governor of Sirhind and told they could live if they gave up their faith. They refused. Tradition says they were walled in with bricks, and then killed. Mata Gujri died soon after, in the cold tower. Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib stands where, tradition says, they were killed. Second, the people who stood near them. Sikh memory keeps the name of the Nawab of Malerkotla, a Muslim ruler who, tradition says, spoke out against killing children, and Sikhs still remember Malerkotla with gratitude. Tradition also remembers a merchant, Todar Mal, who bought ground at great cost so the grandmother and the boys could be cremated with respect. Third, the name. Tradition links Fatehgarh to the younger boy, Fateh. Fateh means victory, the same word in the Sikh greeting, Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh: the Khalsa belongs to God, and so does the victory. So a place of grief carries the word victory. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Kabir says, in paraphrase, that the true warrior is known by fighting for the helpless, and by never leaving the field. Sikh memory says two boys kept that field without lifting a sword. In winter, Sikhs gather here at the Shaheedi Jor Mel, the gathering of the martyrs, to remember them.
screen: `THE GURU'S YOUNGER SONS.` · `THOSE WHO STOOD NEAR THEM.` · `FATEH: VICTORY.` · `NEVER LEAVING THE FIELD.` · then, large: `THE YOUNG MARTYRS.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a small light, light it now; if not, picture one, a single flame in a cold room. Keep company with it, the way the grandmother kept company with the boys, and if someone comes to mind who stood up for a child, let them come. If you pray, you can remember the Sahibzade in your own words.
Fatehgarh Sahib. The gurdwara and town where, tradition says, the Guru's younger sons were killed, and where their name, Fateh, victory, is remembered. Today's word.
Your line: the young martyrs. Two boys, a grandmother, and the strangers who stood near them. Go gently today.

1334.title: Muktsar Sahib
1334.hook: the pool of liberation of the forty
1334.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the forty liberated ones in the Ardas, and gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib each winter for the Maghi mela, bathing in the sarovar and listening to kirtan and the story of the Mukte.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fatehgarh Sahib, the cold tower, and the Guru's younger sons. Your line was the young martyrs.

What does it take to come back, after you've walked away and put it in writing? Not a quiet drift. A signed paper that says: I'm done. That's the story Sikhs tell about a pool in the dry Malwa country of Punjab, once known as Khidrana. Now the town around it is called Muktsar, the pool of liberation, and the people it remembers are the ones who once signed themselves out.
screen: `A SIGNED PAPER: I'M DONE.` → `A POOL CALLED KHIDRANA.` → `NOW: MUKTSAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as tradition tells it. During the long siege of Anandpur, a band of Sikhs from the Majha country lost heart. They wrote a paper, a bedava, saying they were no longer the Guru's Sikhs, and they went home. At home, nobody welcomed them as heroes. A woman named Mai Bhago, tradition says, shamed them for leaving, and then did something harder: she led them back. They found the Guru near the pool of Khidrana, with an army closing in, and they stood between the two. They fought, and they fell. Then comes the moment the story turns on. Tradition says the Guru walked among the fallen and found one of them, Mahan Singh, still breathing. The Guru held him and asked what he wanted. He asked for one thing: tear up the paper. And the Guru tore it. He blessed the men who had come back as mukte, the liberated ones, and the pool took their name. Mukt is liberation; sar is a pool. The Ardas, the prayer Sikhs stand for at the close of their gatherings, still remembers them as the forty liberated ones. Not the men who left: the men who came back. The paper that said they were done is the one thing in the story that doesn't survive. Today a large sarovar lies at the center of the town, with gurdwaras around it, and in winter Sikhs gather there for the Maghi mela, to bathe and to remember.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you stepped away from, a friend, a habit, a practice, a place, and picture the road back, and who might walk it with you, the way Mai Bhago walked with them. You don't have to fix anything. Picture the paper you wrote, out loud or only in your head, that said you were done, and as you breathe out slowly, let it tear.
Muktsar Sahib. The town and pool, once called Khidrana, where tradition says the Guru tore up the paper and blessed the ones who came back as liberated. Today's word.

1335.title: Visiting Goindval
1335.hook: the step-well of Guru Amar Das
1335.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit the baoli at Goindval Sahib, and some recite the Japji Sahib once on each step as they go down to the water, then bathe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muktsar Sahib, where tradition says the Guru tore up the paper of the ones who came back. Your line was the pool of liberation.

The light changes halfway down. At the top of the stairs it's a bright Punjab afternoon, dust and noise and a river nearby. A few steps lower, the walls close in, the air turns cool, and the street drops away. Lower still, there's water, dark and still, at the bottom of a deep shaft of stone. People go down barefoot, one step at a time, some of them saying something under their breath on every step. This is the baoli, the step-well, at Goindval Sahib.
screen: `BRIGHT AT THE TOP.` → `COOL HALFWAY DOWN.` → `WATER AT THE BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: Begin with the place. Goindval is a town on the Beas river, the home of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. Tradition says he had the baoli dug there, so people could reach water in a dry land, and it became a gathering place for Sikhs. Then the purpose. A step-well is a practical thing: water sits deep below the ground, so you build stairs down to it. But a Guru's well was never only plumbing. Tradition says the water was open to everyone, whatever their caste, and that openness was itself a teaching. Next, the custom. Some pilgrims recite the Japji Sahib once on every step as they go down, slowly, all the way to the water. It is slow on purpose. Finally, the Guru's word underneath. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that along this path are the steps of a stairway, and by climbing them one becomes one with the Lord. The Japji's stairs go up; the well's stairs go down. Both say the same thing about how it's done: not in a leap, but one step, then the next, then the next. The baoli at Goindval Sahib still has its stairs, its water, and its slow walkers.

segments.voice: Go to some stairs if they're near, or take a few slow steps across the room, letting each foot land fully before the next and breathing out on every step. If you know a line of the Japji, say it under your breath as you go; if not, just count your breaths, slower than feels normal.
Visiting Goindval. The town of Guru Amar Das on the Beas, and its baoli, where some pilgrims recite the Japji on every step down to the water. Today's word.
Your line: step by step. Nobody reaches the water in a leap. Go gently.

1336.title: Khadur Sahib
1336.hook: where Guru Angad taught the script
1336.howItsDone: Sikhs visit Khadur Sahib to remember Guru Angad and Mata Khivi, and Sikh children learn to read Gurbani in the Gurmukhi script, often starting with the alphabet at a gurdwara Punjabi class.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Goindval and its baoli, walked slowly, one step at a time. Your line was step by step.

How did a child in Punjab learn to write before notebooks were cheap? On a wooden board about the size of a schoolbook, smeared with a pale clay wash and dried in the sun. The child dips a reed pen in ink and writes letters, round and careful. When the board is full, it's washed clean, and the child starts again. Boards like this, called takhtis, are an old way of learning to write in Punjab. And Sikh tradition remembers a Guru who sat with children and their letters, in a small town near the Beas river: Khadur Sahib.
screen: `A WOODEN BOARD, A REED PEN.` → `WRITE, WASH, WRITE AGAIN.` → `KHADUR SAHIB.`

segments.voice: First, the Guru. Khadur was the town of Guru Angad, the second Guru, who took up the work after Guru Nanak. Tradition says he spent his days there among the sangat, with special care for teaching. Second, the script. Tradition says Guru Angad shaped and taught the letters now called Gurmukhi, and wrote out simple primers so children, and grown-ups too, could read the Guru's word for themselves. The Guru Granth Sahib is written in Gurmukhi to this day, so when a Sikh child learns to read Gurbani, the line of teaching runs back, in Sikh memory, to a teacher sitting with children here. Third, the alphabet as a teaching. Guru Nanak had already written a hymn on the letters, the Patti, in which, in paraphrase, each letter becomes a lesson about God and the self. Learning letters and learning the path were never two separate things. Fourth, the kitchen next door. The Guru Granth Sahib, in a ballad of the musicians Satta and Balwand, praises Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife. In paraphrase, she was a good woman whose shade was wide and leafy, and in her langar, rice pudding with ghee was handed out to all. So Khadur Sahib holds both: letters for the mind, and food for anyone who came. Today the town keeps gurdwaras that remember Guru Angad, and children still learn their letters from the same alphabet.

1337.title: Tarn Taran
1337.hook: Guru Arjan's town with one of the largest pools
1337.howItsDone: Pilgrims at Tarn Taran Sahib walk the parikrama around the wide sarovar, bathe in it, and bow at the gurdwara Guru Arjan founded.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khadur Sahib, Guru Angad's town, a schoolroom and a kitchen. Your line was where the script grew.

The Guru is the place of pilgrimage. The Guru is the pool of nectar. That's a paraphrase of a line by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, in the Guru Granth Sahib. Hold it while you stand at the edge of the water at Tarn Taran. The pool is so wide the far side looks small, and the walkway around it, the parikrama, feels like a long evening walk. Along one side, the gurdwara's reflection lies on the water. Guru Arjan made this place. Today: why the town is a pool first.
screen: `THE GURU IS THE POOL OF NECTAR.` → `A WIDE POOL.` → `THE TOWN IS A POOL FIRST.`

segments.voice: Start with the builder. Tradition says Guru Arjan founded Tarn Taran and had its sarovar dug, a pool for bathing and gathering, with the gurdwara beside it. Then the name. Tradition explains Tarn Taran as the boat that carries across, a raft over the world's rough water, so the name points past the water to the crossing. Then the line from the hook, in fuller paraphrase. Guru Arjan writes that the Guru is mother and father, the place of pilgrimage and the pool of nectar, and that bathing in the Guru's wisdom is beyond measure. So the pool at Tarn Taran is a real pool, with real water and real bathers, and also a picture of the Guru's wisdom, wide enough for anyone to step into. Then the people. Tradition says Guru Arjan cared here for people with leprosy, people other towns turned away. A wide pool, and a wide welcome. This is the week's last place, so look back down the road: Panja Sahib, the handprint. Anandpur, the city of bliss. Fatehgarh, the young martyrs. Muktsar, the paper torn up. Goindval, the steps down to the water. Khadur, the letters and the kitchen. And Tarn Taran, the wide pool. Place after place, something ordinary, water, a hand, a paper, a kitchen, a board of letters, turned toward God.

segments.voice: Picture water stretching out so wide the far side looks small, with a walkway of white stone all the way around, and begin to walk it slowly in your mind, the water on your right. Let the people you pass be all kinds, old, young, sick, well, strangers, with room at the edge for all of them, and keep walking and breathing.
Tarn Taran. Guru Arjan's town and its wide sarovar, a name tradition explains as the boat that carries across. Today's word.
Your line: a wide pool. There's room at the edge for one more. That's the week.
